root.note: Kocs is a Hungarian village. A longer phrase, kocsi szekér ‘cart from Kocs’, may have been shortened, but that is less sure.

history: Your coche is named after a village. In the 1400s the Hungarian village of Kocs made horse-drawn vehicles with a new kind of suspension, and a carriage came to be called kocsi, ‘from Kocs’. German made that Kutsche, French made it coche, and Spanish took the French word. When cars arrived, Spain simply moved the old word onto them, and Hungarian did the same. English coach is the same word again. Spanish has no single word here: where Spain says coche, much of Latin America says carro or auto. In Spain, say coche.
historyEinfach: Coche means ‘car’. The word comes from a small village in Hungary called Kocs. People there made good carriages with horses. So the carriage was called kocsi, ‘from Kocs’. The word went to German and French, and then to Spanish. Later, cars took the old word. In much of Latin America, people say carro or auto.

elsewhere.text: English coach is Spanish coche's twin. A sports coach is a later figure of speech: the one who gets you where you need to go.
German kept the old meaning: a Kutsche still has horses. Spanish moved on to cars.
